title: Mathematical Methods II
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Mathematical Methods II curriculum: Fourier series and Fourier transforms, classification of second-order partial differential equations, the heat, wave, and Laplace equations solved by separation of variables, Sturm-Liouville theory, and an introduction to special functions (Legendre polynomials and Bessel functions) and orthogonal function expansions.

questions.question: A Fourier series represents a periodic function f(x) with period 2L as a sum of:
options: sine and cosine terms with frequencies that are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency
questions.correct_answer: sine and cosine terms with frequencies that are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency
questions.explanation: A Fourier series expresses a periodic function as an infinite sum of sines and cosines (harmonics) of the fundamental frequency π/L.

questions.question: For a function f(x) with period 2L, the Fourier coefficient a0 is computed as:
questions.explanation: The standard Fourier coefficient formula gives a0 = (1/L)∫_{-L}^{L} f(x)dx, representing twice the average value of f over one period.

questions.question: The Fourier coefficients an for n ≥ 1 are computed using the formula:
questions.explanation: The cosine coefficients are found by projecting f onto cos(nπx/L) using the standard Fourier integral formula.

questions.question: If f(x) is an odd function, its Fourier series on a symmetric interval contains only:
options: both sine and cosine terms equally
questions.explanation: Since cosine is even and sine is odd, an odd function's Fourier expansion has all an = 0, leaving only the sine (bn) terms.

questions.question: If f(x) is an even function, its Fourier series on a symmetric interval contains only:
options: an equal mix of sine and cosine
questions.explanation: For an even function, all bn = 0 since sine is odd, leaving only the a0 and an cosine terms.

questions.question: At a jump discontinuity x0, the Fourier series of f converges to:
options: the average of the left- and right-hand limits, [f(x0⁻) + f(x0⁺)]/2
questions.correct_answer: the average of the left- and right-hand limits, [f(x0⁻) + f(x0⁺)]/2
questions.explanation: By the Dirichlet convergence theorem, at a jump discontinuity the Fourier series converges to the midpoint of the left and right limits.

questions.question: A half-range Fourier sine series is used to represent a function defined on [0, L] by:
options: extending it as an odd function about x = 0 and periodically
extending it as an even function
restricting it to negative x only
questions.correct_answer: extending it as an odd function about x = 0 and periodically
questions.explanation: A half-range sine expansion treats f as though it were the restriction of an odd, 2L-periodic extension, yielding a pure sine series.

questions.question: The Fourier transform of a function f(t) is defined (in one common convention) as:
questions.explanation: This is the standard integral definition of the Fourier transform, converting a time-domain function into a frequency-domain representation.

questions.question: The Fourier transform generalizes the Fourier series concept from periodic functions to:
options: non-periodic functions defined over the entire real line
functions defined on a finite interval only
questions.correct_answer: non-periodic functions defined over the entire real line
questions.explanation: While Fourier series decompose periodic functions into discrete harmonics, the Fourier transform decomposes general (non-periodic) functions into a continuous spectrum of frequencies.

questions.question: The Fourier transform of the derivative f'(t), assuming f decays at infinity, satisfies:
questions.explanation: This is a key property of the Fourier transform: differentiation in the time domain corresponds to multiplication by iω in the frequency domain.

questions.question: The Convolution Theorem for Fourier transforms states that the Fourier transform of a convolution of two functions equals:
options: the product of their individual Fourier transforms
the sum of their Fourier transforms
questions.correct_answer: the product of their individual Fourier transforms
questions.explanation: Convolution in the time/space domain corresponds to simple multiplication in the frequency domain, a central result used in signal processing and solving PDEs.

questions.question: A second-order linear PDE Auxx + Buxy + Cuyy + ... = 0 is classified as parabolic if:
questions.explanation: This discriminant condition B^2-4AC=0 classifies the PDE as parabolic, analogous to the discriminant test for conic sections; the heat equation is the classic example.

questions.question: The one-dimensional heat equation ut = k uxx is classified as:
questions.explanation: The heat/diffusion equation is the standard example of a parabolic PDE, describing irreversible diffusion processes.

questions.question: The one-dimensional wave equation utt = c^2 uxx is classified as:
questions.explanation: The wave equation is the canonical hyperbolic PDE, modelling phenomena with finite-speed propagation such as vibrating strings.

questions.question: Laplace's equation, uxx + uyy = 0, is classified as:
questions.explanation: Laplace's equation is the standard elliptic PDE, describing steady-state (time-independent) phenomena such as electrostatic potential.

questions.question: The method of separation of variables assumes a solution to a PDE u(x,t) can be written as:
options: u(x,t) = X(x)T(t), a product of single-variable functions
questions.correct_answer: u(x,t) = X(x)T(t), a product of single-variable functions
questions.explanation: Separation of variables seeks solutions in product form, which reduces the PDE to a pair of ordinary differential equations linked by a separation constant.

questions.question: Applying separation of variables to the heat equation ut = k uxx with u=XT leads to the relation:
questions.explanation: Separating variables gives an expression depending only on t equal to one depending only on x; since they're independent variables, both must equal a constant, conventionally written -λ.

questions.question: In solving the heat equation on a finite rod with fixed-temperature (Dirichlet) boundary conditions u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0, the spatial eigenfunctions obtained are:
questions.explanation: Homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions force the spatial solutions to be sine functions satisfying X(0)=X(L)=0, giving eigenfunctions sin(nπx/L).

questions.question: For Laplace's equation on a rectangle with given boundary values, the solution method typically combines:
options: separation of variables with a Fourier series expansion matching the boundary conditions
questions.correct_answer: separation of variables with a Fourier series expansion matching the boundary conditions
questions.explanation: Boundary value problems for Laplace's equation on rectangular domains are classically solved by separating variables and expanding the boundary data in a Fourier series to determine coefficients.

questions.question: A Sturm-Liouville problem has the standard form:
questions.explanation: This is the standard Sturm-Liouville differential equation form, where λ is the eigenvalue parameter and w(x) is the weight function.

questions.question: The eigenvalues of a regular Sturm-Liouville problem are:
options: real and can be ordered as an increasing sequence
questions.correct_answer: real and can be ordered as an increasing sequence
questions.explanation: A key result of Sturm-Liouville theory is that eigenvalues are real and form an increasing, unbounded sequence λ1 < λ2 < λ3 < ...

questions.question: Eigenfunctions of a Sturm-Liouville problem corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are:
options: orthogonal with respect to the weight function w(x)
questions.correct_answer: orthogonal with respect to the weight function w(x)
questions.explanation: A central result of Sturm-Liouville theory is the orthogonality of eigenfunctions belonging to different eigenvalues, under the inner product weighted by w(x).

questions.question: Legendre's differential equation (1-x^2)y'' - 2xy' + n(n+1)y = 0 arises naturally in problems with:
options: spherical symmetry (e.g. solving Laplace's equation in spherical coordinates)
questions.correct_answer: spherical symmetry (e.g. solving Laplace's equation in spherical coordinates)
questions.explanation: Legendre's equation appears when separating variables for Laplace's equation in spherical coordinates, with solutions the Legendre polynomials Pn(cosθ).

questions.question: For nonnegative integer n, the solutions of Legendre's equation that are finite (polynomial) at x = ±1 are called:
questions.explanation: When n is a nonnegative integer, one solution of Legendre's equation reduces to a polynomial of degree n, called the Legendre polynomial Pn(x).

questions.question: The Legendre polynomials Pn(x) satisfy the orthogonality relation on [-1,1]:
options: Pn(x) = Pm(x) for all m, n
Pn(x) is never orthogonal to Pm(x)
questions.explanation: As eigenfunctions of a Sturm-Liouville problem, distinct Legendre polynomials are orthogonal on [-1,1] with weight function 1.

questions.question: The first two Legendre polynomials are P0(x) = 1 and P1(x) =:
questions.explanation: By definition/normalization, P0(x)=1 and P1(x)=x are the first two Legendre polynomials.

questions.question: Bessel's differential equation x^2y'' + xy' + (x^2 - n^2)y = 0 arises typically in problems with:
questions.explanation: Bessel's equation arises when separating variables for the Laplacian in cylindrical coordinates, with solutions Jn(x) called Bessel functions of the first kind.

questions.question: The solutions of Bessel's equation that remain finite at x = 0 (for integer order n) are called:
options: Bessel functions of the first kind, Jn(x)
Bessel functions of the second kind, Yn(x)
questions.correct_answer: Bessel functions of the first kind, Jn(x)
questions.explanation: Jn(x), the Bessel function of the first kind, is the solution that stays bounded at the origin; the second-kind solution Yn(x) diverges there.

questions.question: Bessel functions Jn(x) of different order n satisfy an orthogonality relation with respect to:
options: a weight function x, over an interval determined by the zeros of Jn
questions.correct_answer: a weight function x, over an interval determined by the zeros of Jn
questions.explanation: Bessel functions form an orthogonal set (for fixed order, over different zeros) with respect to the weight x on a finite interval, arising from their Sturm-Liouville structure.

questions.question: A set of functions {φn(x)} is called orthogonal on [a,b] with respect to weight w(x) if:
options: φn(x) = φm(x) for all n, m
questions.explanation: This weighted integral vanishing for distinct indices is the defining condition of orthogonality for a function set.

questions.question: Expanding a function f(x) in terms of an orthogonal set {φn(x)} (a generalized Fourier series) computes the coefficients cn using:
options: cn = (∫ w f φn dx) / (∫ w φn^2 dx)
questions.correct_answer: cn = (∫ w f φn dx) / (∫ w φn^2 dx)
questions.explanation: This generalized Fourier coefficient formula projects f onto each basis function φn, normalized by the squared norm of φn.
